title: Writing a paragraph in German
subtitle: How to write a paragraph at B1–B2 — an opinion, a comparison, a personal story or advice — what the grader looks for and how to deliver it.

text.text: Every attempt is scored on four criteria, and each one counts. A paragraph with perfect grammar that ignores half the prompt scores low; so does a well-organised answer full of agreement errors. Aim for a balance.
— did you answer the prompt, cover every required element, take a clear position where one is asked for, and stay inside the word range?
— does the paragraph have a clear opening, supporting points and a conclusion, and do connectors show how each idea relates to the last?
— is your word choice precise and varied, and does it fit the register (informal or formal) of the task?
— are verb forms, agreement and word order correct, and do you use some more complex structures (subordinate clauses, a range of tenses) accurately?
80–120 words, 15 minutes on the timer.
150–200 words, 25 minutes on the timer.
Going far over the maximum does not earn extra credit — it usually means padding or repetition, and going over the length band also costs you on Task achievement.
Many B1–B2 prompts are open questions with no right answer. Before you write a word, decide
you will answer — then build the whole text around that decision.
There are two. The wording of the prompt usually signals the better fit; when either works, pick the one you can argue best:
— argue one side and answer the strongest objection to it. Use it when the prompt asks for your view: "give your opinion", "do you agree…?", "should…?".
— weigh both sides fairly, then say where you land. Use it when the prompt asks you to "discuss the advantages and disadvantages" or to "compare".

children.text: Either way, commit from the first sentence.

text.text: A balanced answer is not a way to avoid answering: it still ends with a clear judgement.
Both approaches use the same four moves:
— restate the question in your own words, then give your position (stance) or say what you will weigh up (balanced).
— one main reason, backed by an example or a consequence.
— with a stance, raise the strongest counter-argument and answer it; with a balanced view, give the other side fairly.
— answer the question directly. No new arguments.

text.text: At

(150–200 words), write four short paragraphs: an introduction and a conclusion of about 30–40 words each, and two body paragraphs of about 40–55 words each — the primary point usually runs longest. At

(80–120 words), the same four moves fit in 6–8 sentences, one or two per move. Put them in one paragraph or in four very short ones: short paragraphs make the structure visible, and either is fine within 80–120 words.

The question:

children.text: "Sollten Städte Autos aus der Innenstadt verbannen?"

text.text: (should cities ban cars from the city centre?). This answer takes a strong stance. It is 169 words — B2 length (150–200) — in four paragraphs, shown one sentence at a time.

target.text: Immer mehr Städte diskutieren,
Autos in der Innenstadt verboten werden sollten.

body.en: More and more cities are debating whether cars should be banned from the city centre.

note.text: Restates the question in your own words.

target.text: Die Frage ist nicht neu, aber sie wird immer dringender,

body.en: The question is not new, but it is becoming more and more urgent, because traffic keeps increasing.

note.text: Says why the question matters.

target.text: ist ein solches Verbot sinnvoll,

body.en: In my opinion, such a ban makes sense if it is well planned.

note.text: Your position, from the first paragraph.

target.text: Der wichtigste Grund ist die Lebensqualität.

body.en: The most important reason is quality of life.

note.text: The primary point.

target.text: Ohne Autos ist die Luft sauberer, es ist leiser, und Kinder können sicher draußen spielen.

body.en: Without cars the air is cleaner, it is quieter, and children can play outside safely.

note.text: The reason behind it.

target.text: bewegen sich die Menschen mehr, weil sie zu Fuß gehen oder mit dem Rad fahren.

body.en: Moreover, people get more exercise because they walk or cycle.

note.text: A further benefit that supports the same point.

target.text: In Kopenhagen
gibt es seit Jahrzehnten eine Fußgängerzone, in der man ruhig und sicher bummeln kann.

body.en: In Copenhagen, for example, there has been a pedestrian zone for decades where you can stroll in peace and safety.

note.text: A concrete example.

target.text: brauchen manche Menschen das Auto, etwa Handwerker oder ältere Leute,
auch für sie gibt es Lösungen.

body.en: Admittedly, some people need a car, such as tradespeople or older people, but there are solutions for them too.

note.text: Raises the strongest objection and starts to answer it.

target.text: Die Stadt kann den Nahverkehr ausbauen, Parkhäuser am Stadtrand bauen und Sondergenehmigungen für alle ausstellen, die wirklich auf ein Auto angewiesen sind.

body.en: The city can expand local public transport, build multi-storey car parks on the edge of town and issue special permits to everyone who really depends on a car.

note.text: Answers the objection with concrete steps.

target.text: lässt sich sagen,
autofreie Innenstädte deutlich mehr Vorteile als Nachteile haben.

body.en: In conclusion, car-free city centres have far more advantages than disadvantages.

note.text: Answers the question directly.

target.text: Eine Stadt gehört schließlich den Menschen, nicht den Autos.

body.en: After all, a city belongs to people, not to cars.

note.text: Sums up the primary point in one line.

target.text: sollten Städte diesen Schritt wagen, allerdings nicht von heute auf morgen.

body.en: That is why cities should take this step, though not overnight.

note.text: Restates the condition from the introduction — no new argument.

text.text: A strong opinion paragraph has three parts: an
that states your position,
(each backed by a reason or an example, and ideally one point that admits the other side), and a
that restates your view.
The same three-part shape works for every kind of prompt. What changes is the job of the opening sentence:
— states your position.
— names the two things and the point (or points) you will compare them on.
— sets the scene: when, where and who.
— states the problem and your main recommendation.

The supporting points and the closing sentence follow the same pattern: in a comparison, each point compares the two options on one feature, and the closing says which suits whom; in a story, the points are what happened, in order, and the closing says how it ended or what you learned; in advice, each point is a reason or a concrete step.
Here is a model paragraph answering

(are social media good for young people?), one sentence at a time. It is 116 words — B1 length (80–120). A B2 answer needs 150–200 words, so it would develop each point further with an extra reason or example.

target.text: Meiner Meinung nach bringen soziale Medien mehr Nachteile als Vorteile, besonders für Jugendliche.

body.en: In my opinion, social media bring more disadvantages than advantages, especially for young people.

note.text: Opening sentence: states the position clearly.

target.text: verbringen viele junge Menschen täglich mehrere Stunden am Handy,
sie eigentlich lernen sollten.

body.en: Firstly, many young people spend several hours a day on their phones, although they should really be studying.

note.text: Supporting point 1.
takes the first position, so the verb comes second; after
the verb goes to the end.

target.text: vergleichen sie sich ständig mit perfekten Bildern,
das kann ihr Selbstbewusstsein schwächen.

body.en: Moreover, they constantly compare themselves with perfect pictures, and that can weaken their self-confidence.

note.text: Supporting point 2, with a consequence.

target.text: Eine Freundin von mir hat
erzählt,
sie sich nach einer Stunde auf Instagram oft schlecht fühlt.

body.en: A friend of mine told me, for example, that she often feels bad after an hour on Instagram.

note.text: A concrete example backing point 2.
sends
to the end.

target.text: darf man die Vorteile nicht vergessen: Man kann schnell Informationen finden und mit Menschen auf der ganzen Welt sprechen.

body.en: Nevertheless, you must not forget the advantages: you can find information quickly and talk to people all over the world.

note.text: Supporting point 3 admits the other side.

target.text: sollten Eltern und Schulen den Jugendlichen zeigen, wie man soziale Medien bewusst nutzt.

body.en: That is why parents and schools should show young people how to use social media mindfully.

note.text: Draws a consequence from both sides.

target.text: lässt sich sagen, dass soziale Medien für Jugendliche riskant sind,
nützlich sein können, wenn man sie in Maßen nutzt.

body.en: In summary, social media are risky for young people, but they can be useful if used in moderation.

note.text: Closing sentence: restates the position in a more precise form.

text.text: The connectors (highlighted) carry the argument: they tell the reader which sentence is a new point, which is an example, and where the paragraph turns to the other side. They also drive German word order — see the next section.
Here is a model paragraph for a comparison prompt,

children.text: "Ist ein Online-Sprachkurs besser als ein Kurs vor Ort?"

text.text: (is an online language course better than an in-person course?), one sentence at a time. It is 117 words — B1 length (80–120). Each supporting point compares the two options on one feature, and one point names a similarity, not only differences.

target.text: Ein Online-Sprachkurs und ein Kurs vor Ort unterscheiden sich vor allem in drei Punkten: Flexibilität, Kosten und Kontakt zu anderen Lernenden.

body.en: An online language course and an in-person course differ above all in three respects: flexibility, cost and contact with other learners.

note.text: Opening sentence: names the two options and the three points of comparison.

target.text: Online kann man lernen, wann und wo man will,
ein Kurs vor Ort zu festen Zeiten stattfindet.

body.en: Online you can study whenever and wherever you like, whereas an in-person course takes place at fixed times.

note.text: Point of comparison 1 (flexibility).
sends
to the end.

target.text: sind Online-Kurse oft billiger,
die Sprachschule keine Räume mieten muss.

body.en: Moreover, online courses are often cheaper because the language school does not have to rent rooms.

note.text: Point of comparison 2 (cost), with a reason.

target.text: Online-Unterricht bietet ein Kurs vor Ort echten Kontakt: Man spricht in der Pause mit anderen Teilnehmern und übt dabei ganz natürlich.

body.en: Unlike online lessons, an in-person course offers real contact: you talk to other participants during the break and practise without even noticing.

note.text: Point of comparison 3 (contact).
(dative); the whole phrase fills position 1, so the verb
comes next.

target.text: im Kursraum kann man zwar auch online Fragen stellen,
spontane Gespräche sind am Bildschirm viel seltener.

body.en: Just as in the classroom, you can ask questions online, but spontaneous conversations are much rarer on screen.

note.text: Back to contact, this time a similarity, with a limit (

target.text: ist ein Online-Kurs ideal für Menschen mit wenig Zeit,
ein Kurs vor Ort besser für alle ist, die viel sprechen wollen.

body.en: Overall, an online course is ideal for people with little time, whereas an in-person course is better for anyone who wants to speak a lot.

note.text: Closing sentence: says which option suits whom, instead of declaring one simply "better".

text.text: A B2 answer (150–200 words) would extend each point of comparison with an example — a person you know, a price, a typical day.
At B1–B2 the grader looks for
: not just
and
, but connectors that show contrast, consequence and concession — used with the right word order.

target.text: Das Fahrrad ist billig.
ist es gut für die Umwelt.

items.en: The bike is cheap. Moreover, it is good for the environment.

target.text: die Miete hoch ist, wohne ich gern in der Stadt.

items.en: Although the rent is high, I like living in the city.

target.text: in der Stadt immer viel los ist, ist es auf dem Land oft sehr ruhig.

items.en: While there is always a lot going on in the city, it is often very quiet in the countryside.

target.text: Nachts fahren keine Busse.
nehme ich oft ein Taxi.

items.en: There are no buses at night. That's why I often take a taxi.

target.text: Viele Städte,
Kopenhagen, bauen mehr Radwege.

items.en: Many cities, for example Copenhagen, are building more cycle paths.

target.text: kann man sagen, dass beide Seiten gute Argumente haben.

items.en: In summary, one can say that both sides have good arguments.

An informal message to a friend:

target.text: Liebe Anna, wie geht es dir? Ich habe lange nichts von dir gehört.

body.en: Dear Anna, how are you? I haven't heard from you for a long time.

note.text: Informal opening. After the comma, the next line starts in lower case.

target.text: Viele Grüße

body.en: Best wishes

note.text: Informal closing. Also:

text.text: A formal email or letter:

target.text: Sehr geehrte Frau Schmidt,

body.en: Dear Ms Schmidt,

note.text: Formal opening. To an unknown reader:

target.text: ich schreibe Ihnen, weil ich mich für den Sommerkurs interessiere.

body.en: I am writing to you because I am interested in the summer course.

note.text: A standard first line, lower case after the greeting's comma;
capitalised.

target.text: Ich würde mich über eine baldige Antwort freuen.

body.en: I look forward to hearing from you soon.

note.text: Formal pre-closing.

target.text: Mit freundlichen Grüßen

body.en: Yours sincerely

note.text: Formal closing.

sections.title: the task and the word count

text.text: Most prompts list
— things your text must mention. The grader checks each one. Make every element visibly present: give it its own sentence, and use the element's own key word so it cannot be missed.

target.text: Ein Nachteil von sozialen Medien ist, dass sie viel Zeit kosten.

body.en: One disadvantage of social media is that they take up a lot of time.

note.text: Required element "mention a disadvantage" — the key word
makes it impossible to miss.

text.text: Before you write, list the required elements and give each one a sentence. Add your opening and closing sentence to the plan.
Draft the sentences, then join them with connectors so the reasoning is easy to follow.
before you submit, and compare with the range for your level.
Add a reason or a concrete example to your weakest point, or a sentence that admits the other side.
Cut repetition first — sentences that say the same thing twice — not a required element.
These are the errors the grader flags most often at B1–B2. Each example shows the
sentence; the wrong version is in the note.

target.text: Ich glaube, dass das eine gute Idee ist.

body.en: I think that this is a good idea.

note.text: not: *dass das ist eine gute Idee*. In a
clause the verb goes to the end.

target.text: Deshalb habe ich mich für diesen Kurs angemeldet.

body.en: That's why I signed up for this course.

note.text: not: *Deshalb ich habe mich …*. After
at the start, the verb comes second.

target.text: Ich glaube, dass man soziale Medien bewusst nutzen sollte.

body.en: I think that one should use social media mindfully.

note.text: not: *dass man soziale Medien sollte bewusst nutzen*. In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb (here the modal) goes to the very end, after the infinitive.

target.text: Ich lege das Handy auf den Tisch. Jetzt liegt es auf dem Tisch.

body.en: I put the phone on the table. Now it is lying on the table.

note.text: not: *Ich lege das Handy auf dem Tisch*. Two-way prepositions (
…) take the accusative for a destination (
) and the dative for a location (
) — even when there is movement within that place:

target.text: Ich weiß nicht, wann der Zug ankommt.

body.en: I don't know when the train arrives.

note.text: not: *wann der Zug kommt an*. In a subordinate clause, a separable verb joins up again at the end.

Every required element is present, each in its own sentence.
The word count is inside the range for your level.
There is an opening sentence and a closing sentence.
You used at least

ideas — and, for a comparison prompt,
The register is consistent from start to finish — you did not switch between informal and formal.
